newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Frost destroys 5,000 ha sugarbeet in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Frost destroys 5,000 ha sugarbeet in Serbia.

text.p: Frost and low temperatures in Serbia in the past week have destroyed newly-emerging sugar beet plants on some 5,000 hectares, an industry source said Thursday.
"Low temperatures which ranged from minus four to minus 11 degrees Celsius since April 9 have frozen the first sugar beets," said Milan Patkovic, of the sugar producers' association Jugosecer.
"As the low temperatures were registered only in the early morning hours, we managed to re-sow," he told Reuters.
According to Jugosecer, Serbia has planted some 60,000 ha to sugarbeet up to now, well below the official goal of 100,000 ha which would use up the capacity of the country's sugar refineries.
"It is unlikely the beet area will increase any more due to unpaid debts to farmers for their 1996 crop," Patkovic said.
Sugar refineries have concluded deals for beet sowing on 36,325 hectares with publicly owned firms and 26,145 hectares with private farms.
"The final area will not be known until mid-May when we see what damage weeds and pests have wrought," Patkovic added.
According to official statistics, the 1996 beet area was around 70,000 ha.
Jugosecer said the country has enough sugar to bridge the gap till next harvest and meet the needs of its 10.5 million population swollen with refugees.
"A low standard of living reduced annual sugar consumption by 100,000 tonnes to some 300,000 tonnes compared to pre-war years," Patkovic said.
Serbia produced 270,000 tonnes of white sugar from the 1996 beet crop, using 13 of its 15 sugar refineries.
Last year it imported some 180,000 tonnes of raw and white sugar. It also had 50,000 tonnes of white sugar in stock from the 1995 crop.
The sugar surplus was not earmarked for sales abroad due to lower prices on the world market, Patkovic said.
"But we export sugar beet pellets to pay for imports of necessary spare parts and equipment for regular maintainance of refineries". --Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom 381 11 222 4254
